summary.text: Recombination is the era when free electrons and protons first bound together into electrically neutral hydrogen atoms.
It happened about 378,000 years after the Big Bang, once the universe had cooled enough that the radiation could no longer instantly knock atoms apart.
It is a distinct event from photon decoupling, which occurred in the same time frame and is the step that resulted in the cosmic microwave background radiation.

facts.label: When it happened
facts.value: About 378,000 years after the Big Bang

facts.label: Name is misleading
facts.value: Protons and electrons had never been combined before

facts.label: Early models
facts.value: Peebles and Zel'dovich's team, independently in 1968

facts.label: Neutral by
facts.value: The universe was 90% neutral at about z = 1070

items.prompt: A student says recombination means electrons and protons were joined once, split apart, and then joined again. Is this right?

options.label: Yes, atoms formed, broke apart and re-formed
No, they had not been combined before; the name is historical
Yes, but only helium atoms were involved
No, because electrons never combine with protons

items.explain: The Big Bang theory does not say protons and electrons were combined earlier. The name was chosen before that theory became the main one.

items.prompt: Just before recombination, energetically favoured atoms still could not last. What stopped them?

options.label: There were too few electrons to join protons
Hydrogen refused to bond at any temperature
The protons moved too fast to catch electrons
The huge number of photons would immediately ionize them

items.explain: Atoms could form energetically, but one of the vast number of photons would immediately ionize them, until the universe cooled enough.

items.prompt: Imagine two clocks, one marking atoms forming and one marking light starting to travel freely. They tick at nearly the same moment. Are they the same event?

options.label: Yes, atoms forming is how light is freed
Yes, they are two names for one process
No, they happen at the same time but rest on different physical processes
No, photon decoupling came billions of years later

items.explain: They occurred in the same time frame, but are distinct events based on different physical processes.

items.prompt: What lets the huge number of photons travel without scattering, so that they become the cosmic microwave background?

options.label: Expansion thins out the free electrons
Photons turn into matter as they cool
Helium absorbs them all
Electrons grow heavier and slow down

items.explain: Photon decoupling happened when expansion diluted the electrons, so the photons could propagate without scattering.

items.prompt: A fast shortcut for forming hydrogen would be an electron dropping straight to the lowest energy level. Why does this work poorly?

options.label: It needs far more electrons than exist
It releases a photon that almost immediately re-ionizes a nearby atom
It makes the atom too heavy to stay together
It only works for helium and not for hydrogen

items.explain: Each direct recombination to the ground state gives off a photon above 13.6 eV, which almost immediately re-ionizes a neighbouring hydrogen atom.

items.prompt: Today's microwave background is at 2.7 K, and the shift is given by T = 2.7 K × (1 + z). Roughly how did the temperature at z = 1100 compare with today's?

options.label: About the same temperature
About 1,100 times cooler
About 1,100 times hotter
About 11 times hotter

items.explain: With T = 2.7 K × (1 + z), a redshift of z = 1100 means the temperature was about 1,101 times today's.
